title: SQL & Database Mastery Test
description: Test your relational SQL mastery: aggregations, joins, subqueries, indexing, constraints, and transactions.

questions.question: What is the difference between `DELETE FROM users;` and `TRUNCATE TABLE users;`?
options: `DELETE` removes rows one-by-one and logs each deletion in the transaction log (can be rolled back); `TRUNCATE` deallocates data pages instantly as DDL
`TRUNCATE` deletes the table structure completely
`DELETE` is faster than `TRUNCATE`
`TRUNCATE` allows a `WHERE` clause
questions.explanation: TRUNCATE is a high-speed DDL operation that resets identity counters and deallocates data pages with minimal transaction logging.

questions.question: What is the difference between `UNION` and `UNION ALL` in SQL?
options: `UNION` removes duplicate rows from the combined result set (with sort overhead); `UNION ALL` retains all duplicates and is faster
`UNION ALL` only works on two tables with identical primary keys
`UNION` joins tables horizontally; `UNION ALL` vertically
There is no difference in modern SQL databases
questions.explanation: UNION runs a distinct sorting pass to eliminate duplicate rows, while UNION ALL simply appends results together directly.

questions.question: In SQL window functions, what is the difference between `RANK()` and `DENSE_RANK()`?
options: `RANK()` skips rank values after a tie (e.g. 1, 2, 2, 4); `DENSE_RANK()` does not skip values (e.g. 1, 2, 2, 3)
`DENSE_RANK()` only ranks strings; `RANK()` ranks numbers
`RANK()` requires a PARTITION BY clause while `DENSE_RANK()` does not
`DENSE_RANK()` assigns negative numbers to ties
questions.explanation: RANK produces gaps in ranking sequences when ties occur, whereas DENSE_RANK assigns consecutive integers without gaps.

questions.question: What does the `COALESCE(val1, val2, val3)` function return in SQL?
options: The first non-null expression among its arguments
The concatenation of all string values
The arithmetic average of numeric values
The largest numerical value
questions.explanation: COALESCE evaluates arguments in sequence and returns the first value that is not NULL, or NULL if all are null.

questions.question: What is a Composite (Compound) Index in a relational database?
options: An index built on two or more columns of a table, which can be used by queries filtering on the leftmost prefix of those columns
An index that automatically compresses table rows into zip files
An index that spans across two distinct database servers
An index that only works on foreign keys
questions.explanation: Composite indexes index multiple columns (e.g. `(last_name, first_name)`). Queries must filter by the leftmost columns to benefit from the index.

questions.question: What does a Common Table Expression (CTE) defined with `WITH` achieve in SQL?
options: Defines a temporary named result set within the execution scope of a single SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE statement
Creates a permanent table stored on physical disk
Backs up table records to a cloud storage bucket
Encrypts the column values in memory
questions.explanation: CTEs simplify complex nested subqueries and enable recursive hierarchical queries (e.g. organizational trees).

questions.question: What happens when you execute `SELECT COUNT(*)` versus `SELECT COUNT(column_name)` on a table with some NULL values in `column_name`?
options: `COUNT(*)` counts all rows including NULLs; `COUNT(column_name)` counts only rows where `column_name` is NOT NULL
Both return the exact same count number
`COUNT(column_name)` throws an error on encountering NULL
`COUNT(*)` only counts primary key columns
questions.explanation: `COUNT(*)` counts total rows in the result set, while `COUNT(column)` ignores null values in that specific column.

questions.question: What is a 'Phantom Read' anomaly during concurrent database transactions?
options: Transaction A reads a set of rows satisfying a condition; Transaction B inserts new matching rows and commits; Transaction A re-executes the query and sees new 'phantom' rows
A transaction reads uncommitted changes from another transaction (Dirty Read)
A transaction modifies data that was deleted by the operating system
A query returns cached results after the server restarted
questions.explanation: Phantom reads occur when a transaction re-reads a range of rows and finds additional rows inserted by another committed transaction.

questions.question: What is Database Normalization (e.g. 3rd Normal Form - 3NF)?
options: Organizing database tables and columns to minimize data redundancy and prevent insert/update/delete anomalies
Converting all strings to lowercase in the database
Scaling database servers across 3 geographic zones
Backing up database tables every 3 hours
questions.explanation: 3NF ensures every non-key attribute is non-transitively dependent on the primary key, preventing duplicate data storage and inconsistencies.

questions.question: In SQL, what is the purpose of the `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` command?
options: Executes the query and displays the actual query execution plan, node timings, rows scanned, and index usage details
Checks SQL syntax without running the query
Automatically optimizes and rewrites slow queries
Translates SQL queries into Python code
questions.explanation: `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` runs the statement and outputs detailed profiling data showing sequential scans, index scans, hash joins, and actual execution time per node.
